# SHOUT — Stop Home Owners' Unfair Tax
# https://shoutunfairtax.uk

> SHOUT is an independent grassroots campaign opposing the High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS), often referred to as the "Mansion Tax" — a proposed annual levy on residential properties in England valued at £2 million and above, based on 2026 Valuation Office Agency assessments. The campaign has no political affiliation.

## What is the HVCTS?

The High Value Council Tax Surcharge (HVCTS) was announced in the UK Autumn Budget on 26 November 2025 by Chancellor Rachel Reeves. From April 2028, homeowners of residential properties in England valued at or above £2 million will pay an annual surcharge on top of their existing council tax bill. The Government estimates 145,000 to 165,000 homeowners will be affected.

Annual surcharge bands:
- £2m – £2.5m: £2,500 per year
- £2.5m – £3.5m: £3,500 per year
- £3.5m – £5m: £5,000 per year
- £5m and above: £7,500 per year

Rates will increase with CPI annually from 2029-30. The tax will raise approximately £400 million per annum — less than 15 hours of HMRC's annual tax take.

## Campaign Position

SHOUT does not oppose fair taxation. The campaign opposes this specific policy on the grounds that it is:
- Arbitrary in design and regressive in real-world impact
- Harmful to asset-rich, cash-poor homeowners, including retirees on fixed incomes
- Disproportionately affecting London and South East homeowners due to local property values, not exceptional wealth
- Based on a flawed and untested VOA valuation methodology
- Subject to threshold creep — ATED started at £2m and was reduced to £500,000 within three years
- Contrary to long-established UK taxation principles (assets taxed on sale, not on paper value)

## Historical Context

- Dennis Healey abandoned a similar wealth tax in 1976, admitting it was "impossible to draft one which would yield enough revenue to be worth the administrative cost and political hassle"
- Austria, Denmark and Germany abandoned wealth taxes in 1997; Finland and Luxembourg in 2006; Sweden in 2007; Iceland in 2014
- France abolished its broad-based ISF wealth tax in 2018 under President Macron
